meta: To learn, AI has to know how wrong it is. Like throwing darts: the distance to the bullseye is a number that measures the miss. That number is called the error, or the loss function.
prompt: Under 100 words, friendly tone, end with an invitation

muc.title: How wrong?
muc.text: Last time: AI learns by turning billions of knobs. But to turn them the right way, the machine has to know how wrong it is. So how is "wrong" measured?

muc.title: Throwing darts
muc.text: Picture throwing darts at a target. Hitting the bullseye is right. The farther you miss, the more wrong you are. The distance to the bullseye is a number that measures the miss.

muc.title: A number that measures being wrong
muc.text: AI works the same way. The machine gives an answer and compares it with the right one. How far off it is becomes a number, called the error, or the loss function.

muc.title: A photo of a cat
muc.text: Show the machine a photo of a cat. It says: 70% dog. The loss is very big. Next time it says: 90% cat. The loss is much smaller.

muc.title: Push the number down
muc.text: The whole learning process aims at one thing: push this error number as low as possible. Every time it turns the knobs, the machine checks whether the loss went up or down.

muc.title: You get what you measure
muc.text: But the machine only optimizes exactly what's measured, nothing more. If essays are graded only by length, it will learn to write long, not better.

muc.title: Say clearly what good means
muc.text: When you ask AI for something, you're giving it a measuring stick too. Don't just say "write it better". Say exactly: under 100 words, friendly tone, end with an invitation. The clearer the criteria, the closer AI gets.

muc.title: Which way to fix it?
muc.text: Now it knows it's wrong. But with billions of knobs, which way should it turn them? The answer is like walking down a mountain in the fog. See you in part 3.
